title: Filmmakers Hail 'Ramayana' as India's 'Lord of the Rings' as Epic Opens Worldwide
excerpt: Nitesh Tiwari's two-part epic, made over more than a decade with a reported $420 million combined budget, draws praise from Rajamouli, Vanga and Rishab Shetty — and an opening-day India take of Rs 64.85 crore.
body:
• "Ramayana: Rise of a Legend," directed by Nitesh Tiwari and starring Ranbir Kapoor as Rama, Sai Pallavi as Sita and Yash as Ravana, opened in cinemas worldwide on Thursday, November 5, in Hindi and English versions.
  • Producer Namit Malhotra has branded the two-part production India's own "Star Wars" or "Lord of the Rings"; AFP reports a combined budget of about $420 million and more than a decade in the making.
  • SS Rajamouli, Sandeep Reddy Vanga and Rishab Shetty have publicly praised the film's scale and the lead performances; trade tracker Sacnilk put opening-day India nett collections at Rs 64.85 crore.
  • The score is by Hans Zimmer and A. R. Rahman, the visual effects are by DNEG, and Sony Pictures is the international distributor — US audiences can watch it in theatres now.

India's most expensive bet on its oldest story is now in cinemas. "Ramayana: Rise of a Legend" opened worldwide on Thursday, November 5, after more than a decade in the making, and filmmakers in India and abroad are hailing it in the terms its producer chose for it: as India's answer to "The Lord of the Rings," AFP reported.

The film adapts the Sanskrit epic: Rama, played by Ranbir Kapoor, battles to rescue his kidnapped wife Sita, played by Sai Pallavi, from the demon king Ravana, played by Yash, who also co-produces. It is directed by Nitesh Tiwari and made by Malhotra's Mumbai-based Prime Focus Studios with Yash's Monster Mind Creations. The movie has Hindi and English versions, and Sony Pictures is handling international distribution.

The scale behind the comparison

Producer Namit Malhotra calls it the largest production in the history of Indian cinema — his words, offered as the film's ambition rather than an audited record — and has branded it India's "Star Wars" or "Lord of the Rings." AFP reports a combined budget of about $420 million for the planned two parts. Malhotra's UK-headquartered visual effects arm DNEG, which built the film's world, has won eight Academy Awards for work on films including "Inception" and "Dune." The score is shared by two Oscar-winning composers, Hans Zimmer and A. R. Rahman, and the film sets aside the song-and-dance routines of traditional Bollywood in favour of spectacle.

"East and West have come together in a true sense."

— Yash, co-producer and Ravana in "Ramayana," to AFP

For Tiwari, the point of the exercise was the text itself. "There's a certain sense of timelessness to the emotions and the values which Ramayana stands for and that is exactly what we wanted to bring to the rest of the world," he told AFP.

Filmmakers weigh in

The praise from fellow directors has been specific. SS Rajamouli wrote that the scale and visuals are spectacular on the big screen, calling Kapoor serene yet magnificent from the Vanavasam sequence onward, Yash menacing as Ravana and Sai Pallavi graceful as Sita, and singled out the pre-climax and climax. Sandeep Reddy Vanga urged audiences to experience the magnitude of Ram and Raavana on the big screen and said both leads nailed their roles. Rishab Shetty said the makers had done total justice to the timeless epic and praised Kapoor's calm, grace and dignity as Rama, according to MensXP's roundup of the directors' posts.

What the diaspora reader needs to know

The film is a two-part spectacle, with the second part reported to be headed for 2028. Trade tracker Sacnilk, via MensXP, put the opening-day India nett collection at Rs 64.85 crore, and our earlier coverage tracked the film toward Rs 450 crore worldwide by its fourth day. For US readers, the practical facts are these: the film is in theatres now in both Hindi and English versions, it runs as the first half of a two-part story, and its makers are pitching it as Indian cinema's global breakout attempt — a film built, in Malhotra's framing, to be judged against Hollywood's biggest franchises rather than against other Hindi releases.
